label: ideas, scholarship
q: What did Marshall McLuhan's laws of media (the tetrad) actually claim, how have scholars applied, extended or criticised it since Laws of Media appeared in 1988, and has anyone tried to test it empirically?

report.title: The Tetrad After the Fact: What McLuhan's Laws of Media Claimed, What Scholars Did With Them, and Whether Anyone Tested Them

review.sentence: That framing matters for judging the tetrad on its own terms: it is offered as the recovery of a pre-Aristotelian, fourfold, analogical mode of knowing, not as a hypothesis in the social-scientific sense.
review.why: The cited publisher's description [2] says the opposite in the very next sentence: "The laws identified by the McLuhans consitute a new scientific basis for media studies, testable, and able to allow for prediction." The blurb cannot be used to show the book is not offered as a social-scientific hypothesis.

review.sentence: So the tetrad is not a theory of media change with a temporal mechanism.
review.why: The publisher's blurb [2] promises the laws are "testable, and able to allow for prediction", and the practitioner gloss the section itself quotes [8] says reversal effects "may not be realized until the figure fades into the ground and becomes ubiquitous" — an effect that unfolds over time. The laws being simultaneous does not make the tetrad atemporal.

review.sentence: It also shows the characteristic weakness: "the sender is sent" is a compressed figure, not an observable, and nothing in the example says what would count as the claim being wrong.
review.why: The section discusses the cell-phone tetrad as the cleanest illustration but leaves out the McLuhans' own wine tetrad (Laws of Media p. 206), where they give two different, incompatible sets of answers for the same artefact on the same page — the most direct evidence about what the tetrad actually yields and about its reliability (Tyler 2008).

review.sentence: The wording that has circulated most widely comes from the publisher's description of the 1988 book, which is also the form in which most later writers quote it: "What does it enhance or intensify? What does it render obsolete or displace? What does it retrieve that was previoulsy obsolesced? What does it produce or become when pressed to an extreme?" [2].
review.why: Source [2] only supplies the blurb text; no note supports the claims that this wording "circulated most widely" or that it is how "most later writers" quote the laws.

review.sentence: Writing before the book appeared, Tom Tyler summarised the 1970s journal versions as four numbered laws: a technology amplifies or enhances some aspect of human experience or society; it obsolesces some aspect; it retrieves some aspect; and it reverses or flips into something else [6].
review.why: The cited article is Tyler's "A Procrustean Probe", Game Studies 8(2), December 2008 — twenty years after Laws of Media — so he was not writing before the book appeared. Only the substance of the four laws, not the dating, comes from the source.

review.sentence: Levinson, who wrote the preface to the 1977 *ETC* publication of the laws, organised the 1978 tetrad conference and proposed "tetrad wheels" — chains in which one tetrad's reversal becomes the next medium's point of departure, so that a series of fourfolds describes a historical trajectory.
review.why: No note in the record mentions Levinson, tetrad wheels, the ETC preface or a 1978 conference: [6] is Tyler's Game Studies article and [9] is the Library and Archives Canada page, neither of which names him. The section itself concedes it is reporting a "previous research pass" rather than a read text, so the central claim of the "chaining" programme rests on nothing in the notes.

review.sentence: Each quadrant is anchored in cited research rather than in the analyst's impressions: enhancement engages Putnam's *Bowling Alone* and Arthur Asa Berger, obsolescence engages European and Kaiser Family Foundation media-use studies and Nick Yee's MMORPG data.
review.why: Tyler's paper cites no Kaiser Family Foundation study anywhere; the media-use evidence in the obsolescence section is Beentjes et al.'s 2001 cross-European study, Yee's Daedalus data, and (in the endnotes) Pratchett et al., the UK ONS and Fromme. The Kaiser Foundation attribution appears invented.

review.sentence: His essay ends with a deliberate reductio that has become the most-quoted sentence in the applied literature: "The Internet intensifies identity politics, renders identity politics obsolete, retrieves identity politics and may flip into identity politics" [3][6].
review.why: The quotation is in [3], but nothing in the record measures its reception, and [6] does not mention Eriksen at all. "Most-quoted sentence in the applied literature" is an unverifiable claim about citation impact, not something the sources show.

review.sentence: Across four decades the tetrad has been applied to wine, the cell phone, the Internet at three levels, CD-ROMs, LP records, aeroplanes, smartphones, Zoom, Microsoft Teams, digital games, cop-watching video, soundscape composition, laser cleaning machines and media art.
review.why: Wine, the cell phone, the Internet, CD-ROMs, LP records, aeroplanes, smartphones, games and cop-watching are all in the notes; Zoom, Microsoft Teams, soundscape composition and laser cleaning machines appear in no note in the record, so half the breadth of this survey sentence has no support.

review.sentence: He narrows his scope deliberately, confining enhancement to solo-play complexity, and he claims modestly that the result is one amongst many possible surveys [1][6].
review.why: Tyler confines himself to solo play only "for a moment" and then devotes a long passage to multiplayer gaming, arguing that computerisation also enhances play with others "on an unprecedented scale". The enhancement analysis is not confined to solo-play complexity, which weakens the praise being given here.

review.sentence: Read this way the tetrad is a diagnostic for bringing an organisation's unnoticed environment into view — the figure/ground relation that Harman identifies as one of the tetrad's two generating dualisms [10].

sentences.sentence: What does it produce or become when pressed to an extreme?" [2].
What does it render obsolete…" — as a search of the text of *Laws of Media* confirms [7].

Tom Tyler, writing in 2007 and 2008, summarised the 1970s journal versions as four numbered laws: a technology amplifies or enhances some aspect of human experience or society; it obsolesces some aspect; it retrieves some aspect; and it reverses or flips into something else [6].

A practitioner restatement from 2007 shows how the last two are commonly glossed: "Every medium retrieves, in some new form, the idea of a previously obsolescent medium" [8], and "Every medium, when stretched to the limits of its capability, reverses into the opposite of its original effect" [8].

The publisher's description makes "medium" coextensive with any human artefact or idea, and states the claim in its strongest form: "Inherent in every human innovation is an answer to each of the questions of this tetrad; anything that does not contain answers to these four questions is not the product of human creation" [2].
Eliot and James Joyce in this century" [2].

The blurb carries two claims at once, and they pull in opposite directions: the tetrad retrieves an older, pre-Aristotelian way of knowing, and it is also "a new scientific basis for media studies, testable, and able to allow for prediction" [2].

The book is posthumous — Marshall McLuhan died in 1980, and the 1988 volume was completed with Eric McLuhan [2] — so the canonical statement of the tetrad is also the least author-supervised one. **Simultaneity, not sequence.** The single most misunderstood feature is that the four laws are not stages.
Although McLuhan sometimes talked about them as succeeding each other, he did not intend for them to be considered in a chronological order" [9].

Tyler records the same point from the book, at page 99, and draws the consequence: because the laws operate simultaneously rather than sequentially, the tetrad works as a heuristic device for interrogating what is implicit or "inherent" within a medium [6].

Simultaneity does not make the tetrad atemporal, though: the publisher promises that the laws allow for prediction [2], and practitioner glosses describe reversal as arriving only once a medium's figure has faded into the ground and become ubiquitous [8].
Reversal when pushed to extremes: letters, and "the sender is sent" [9].

The wine tetrad on page 206 of the same book is the sharper evidence about what the method actually yields, because there the McLuhans answer all four questions twice over, incompatibly, on a single page — a case taken up in sections 3 and 5 [1][3]. **What the tetrad therefore claims, stated plainly.** Four things, in ascending order of strength.
Second, that these four descriptions are of simultaneous features of one situation, not a causal sequence [6][9].
Fourth, that the set is complete and universal, so that an artefact lacking an answer to any of the four is not a human artefact at all [2].
Tyler records that McLuhan asserted the four laws were testable hypotheses and a scientific method modelled on Popper's principle of falsifiability, citing the 1975 and 1977 papers [6].

The 1977 version in *ETC: A Review of General Semantics* — published with a preface by Paul Levinson — carried the same claim, and Tyler quotes its description of the laws as a "rigorous means of investigating" the effects of artefacts on people and society [6].
The University of Toronto Press description of *Laws of Media: The New Science* calls the laws "a new scientific basis for media studies, testable, and able to allow for prediction" [2].

It is also the claim that later scholarship treats as the tetrad's official position — and it is worth being precise that "testable" and "able to allow for prediction" appear in marketing copy, not in a sentence the McLuhans wrote for the book. **The strongest internal version.** Inside the book, the checkability claim is put even more aggressively, by Eric McLuhan: the four questions "can be asked (and the answers checked) by anyone, anywhere, at any time, about any human artefact" [1][6].

Library and Archives Canada's account, citing *Laws of Media* page 116, says flatly that "The tetrad is not meant to be a scientific tool" — it is a dynamic tool for describing situations that are in process [9].
Tyler's verdict is that calling these scientific laws, in anything like the ordinary sense of the term, is preposterous — and yet, he adds, the tetrad has its uses [1].

His constructive move is to take McLuhan at his word elsewhere: the tetrad is most effective as a probe, a means of investigation, and McLuhan's own formula was that he does not explain but explores [1].
The publisher says the laws are testable and predictive [2].
Eric McLuhan says the answers can be checked by anyone, anywhere [1].
Library and Archives Canada says the tetrad is not a scientific tool [9].
In the second, wine enhances food and the occasion, obsolesces inhibition, retrieves the festive spontaneity of speech and gesture, and reverses into hangover and insult [1][3].

Tyler draws the inference directly: if the authors themselves seem unsure about the consistency of the results, it seems unlikely that the same results will be achieved by anyone, anywhere, at any time [1].

His sentence is worth having in full because it is the version later critics quote: as a universal scientific method, the tetrad is far too vague, since "a sufficiently creative mind can imagine, for almost any human artefact, a huge range of things which it might be considered to augment, obsolesce, retrieve, and reverse into" [1][3].
Tyler's formulation: "it requires us to fill the gaps" [1][3].

He then tests this against the wine example, asking whether we really want to say that wine obsolesces commonplace flavours or retrieves ritual observance, and answering that the analysis does violence to these complex notions when they are forced into the tetrad's frame [1][3].
He names the move with Nietzsche's phrase about fitting new material into old schemes — making equal what is new [1][3].

The double bind is the real finding: an instrument that is simultaneously unfalsifiable (any answer is admissible) and coercive (an answer must be produced) cannot be corrected by evidence in either direction. **The verdict, and the concession.** Tyler's summary judgement is that calling these scientific laws in anything like the ordinary sense is preposterous — followed immediately by the concession that the tetrad has its uses [1][3].

His closing standard is aesthetic and pragmatic rather than epistemic: "The danger with any theory or schema is that it inevitably does violence to its subject matter" [1], and that violence is redeemed only if the resulting analysis is constructive — if the probe works for us as the bed did for Theseus rather than as it did for Procrustes [1][3].
Once the scientific rhetoric is dropped, he argues, divergent tetrads for the same artefact are not a defect so long as they yield illuminating insight [1][3].
On his reading, enhancement and obsolescence together constitute what the McLuhans call the morphology of an artefact, while retrieval and reversal constitute its metamorphosis [10].

The morphology, he argues, already incorporates in practical form Heidegger's critique of presence-at-hand — the point that a thing's readiness-to-hand is not exhausted by its measurable properties [10].

First, he states the universality claim as strongly as the publisher does: "every human artifact does four separate things simultaneously" — it enhances something, makes something else obsolete, retrieves a previously dead medium, and eventually reverses into its opposite [10].
His own identification of the tetrad's dualisms is morphology — the pairing of enhancement with obsolescence — and metamorphosis, the pairing of retrieval with reversal [10].

Third, he offers a friendly correction to the McLuhans' own wording: they sometimes write as though "enhance" meant making something more visible, whereas on their own principles it should mean making something into more of a hidden medium while downplaying its visible content [10].
Reversal, he says, is largely outside our control, while retrieval is the cell in which deliberate human agency operates [10].

Harman is explicit that the stakes include McLuhan's academic standing: he notes that the majority rejection of McLuhan's canonical status rests on either the charge of flashy punditry or the charge of technological determinism exposed by Raymond Williams [10], and his essay is partly an argument that both charges misread the work.

The determinism charge — that the tetrad's language of what a medium does leaves no room for users — is the one Harman attributes to Williams and answers by pointing to the retrieval cell's dependence on human choice [10].

Its interest is structural: it reintroduces sequence into an instrument whose four laws are supposed to operate simultaneously [6][9], which makes the tetrad usable for history at the cost of a construction the tetrad itself does not license. **Anthropology: Eriksen's three-level tetrads.** The earliest substantial post-publication application I found is Thomas Hylland Eriksen's 1996 web essay, and it is unusually honest about the instrument's status.

Eriksen calls the laws "overambitiously phrased and deterministic" and argues only that they may help create distinctions between different kinds of effects — if so, it can be worthwhile to try them out [3][6].
His essay ends with a deliberate reductio: "The Internet intensifies identity politics, renders identity politics obsolete, retrieves identity politics and may flip into identity politics" [3].

He describes the tetrad as arrived at by asking the four questions out of historical, social and technological knowledge of the subject [5], and notes that it is commonly displayed graphically with the four elements as points of change on a continuum [5].
He also quotes McLuhan and Powers on the tetrad performing the function of myth by compressing past, present and future into one through simultaneity [5].

Federman's restatement of the premise is the clearest statement of what the tetrad is for in that setting: McLuhan was concerned that "we tend to focus on the obvious", and in doing so we largely miss the structural changes introduced subtly, or over long periods of time [11].

The figure/ground vocabulary here is Federman's, not Harman's: Harman's two generating dualisms are morphology and metamorphosis [10], and figure/ground is the perceptual pair the McLuhan tradition uses alongside them.

It calls the tetrad a "scientific model" and a tool applicable to any technology or artefact [4]; it asserts that McLuhan developed it late in life as a summing-up of his ideas [4]; it holds that although the tetrad was developed three decades earlier it is universal in nature and therefore still applicable to present and future technological developments, its value consisting in bringing the four laws together and so looking simultaneously at past, present and future, at the medium itself and at its context [4].
It also states the universality claim in its strongest form: the four effects are, according to McLuhan, inevitable and apply universally [4].
It concedes that multiple interpretations are possible when applying the tetrad, since one's interpretation is always based on one's own thoughts and perceptions [4][6].

It fills the reversal cell with what it openly calls speculation — the tetrad allows one to reflect on the past and to try to predict, or at least speculate, about future developments [4] — and it concedes that one cannot say with certainty what McLuhan would say [4].

Its empirical content is entirely borrowed: studies of the Google effect and of nomophobia about smartphone effects in general, not evidence bearing on whether the four laws hold of the smartphone [4].

Where the evidence does not settle a cell he says so, concluding that the existing studies of whether games displace television are collectively uncertain and that none is by any means conclusive [1][6], and he then redefines obsolescence as remediation in the Bolter-and-Grusin sense rather than forcing the original claim.

He narrows his scope deliberately at the outset, and though he later extends the enhancement analysis to multiplayer play, he claims modestly that the result is one amongst many possible surveys [1][6].

Drawing primarily on McLuhan, they argue that the medium is the message and that video clips of police actions shared through the internet may actually neutralise, to some extent, the political potential of cop-watching, so that caution is warranted about over-emphasising the power of video activism [14].

The direction is coherent with the tetrad's design: if the four cells are prompts, a language model can fill them fluently and at scale, which is exactly the "sufficiently creative mind" whose existence Tyler's looseness objection depends on [1][3].
Almost every application is by a single analyst, cites no second coder, and treats divergent results as a feature [4].

I searched for reliability studies, coding schemes, expert panels, Delphi applications and quasi-experiments, and found none that treats the tetrad itself as the object of measurement. **What would count as a test, and why the claim makes it possible.** The tetrad's own literature supplies a testable proposition even where its authors disclaim science: Eric McLuhan's claim that the four questions can be asked and the answers checked by anyone, anywhere, at any time, about any human artefact [1][6].

Two tetrads for the same artefact, on the same page, sharing no cell: enhancement is grape juice in one version and food and the occasion in the other; obsolescence is commonplace flavours against inhibition; retrieval is ritual observance against festive spontaneity of speech and gesture; reversal is cooking wine vinegar against hangover and insult [1][3].

Tyler's inference is the reliability conclusion stated in words: if the authors themselves seem unsure about the consistency of the results, it seems unlikely that the same results will be achieved by anyone, anywhere, at any time [1].
If anything that lacks answers to the four questions is not a human artefact at all [2], then no artefact can supply a negative case.

A proposition that no observation could refute is not a candidate for testing, and the tetrad's defenders state it in exactly this form: every human artefact does four things simultaneously [10], and the four effects are inevitable and apply universally [4].

Eriksen's Internet example enters the same item in all four quadrants — the Internet intensifies identity politics, renders identity politics obsolete, retrieves identity politics and may flip into identity politics [3][6].

The peer-reviewed smartphone application states that multiple interpretations are possible because one's interpretation is always based on one's own thoughts and perceptions [4][6] — a candid statement that the instrument's output is a function of the analyst.

In the same essay the reversal cell is filled with what the author calls speculation about future developments [4], which is the cell where an empirical criterion would be most valuable and where it is most conspicuously absent.
He urged that one should never predict anything that has not already happened [1][6].

Its abstract states the aim plainly: the tetrad, historically limited to media theory, consists of four basic interrelated questions that McLuhan held to be fundamental to technologies, and "The objective of this thesis is to demonstrate that the tetrad can be applied to an analysis of other forms of innovation" [13].

The intended application is commercial: a product-development team, asking what an innovation enhances and then working through the remaining three cells, would be enabled to focus on the innovation's probable future effects and resultant consumer needs, giving planners and innovators a tool to reveal the consequences of innovation [13].

He reviews comparative media-use research, including a 2001 cross-European study that asked whether interactive media had substantially changed children's media time expenditure, and which found that electronic games had taken the third position behind television and audio media previously held by print, at least among boys, with the impact on television unclear; the authors warn that their cross-sectional data are unfit to determine causal relationships between media [1][6].
Tyler's conclusion is that none of these studies is by any means conclusive [1][6].

I did not read that study directly for this report, so I cite it as reported there rather than as a primary finding, but it bears precisely on the tetrad's failure mode: a sufficiently creative mind can fill the cells, and filling them well is not the same as being right [1][3].

Strip out the definitional guarantee.** The publisher's statement that anything lacking answers to the four questions is not a product of human creation [2] has to go, because it makes every case a confirming case.

Tyler's own tetrad is the model here: he reports that the evidence on whether games displace television is collectively uncertain and that none of the studies is by any means conclusive [1][6], and then redefines the cell rather than filling it.
Constrain the answer space before coding.** Tyler's looseness objection is that a sufficiently creative mind can imagine a huge range of candidates for any cell [1][3].

This is the step Eriksen's essay shows to be indispensable and missing: his three tetrads for the Internet at technological, social and cultural levels are not comparable, because no rule fixes the level [3][6].

Make the cells mutually exclusive.** Eriksen's reductio — the Internet intensifies, obsolesces, retrieves and flips into identity politics [3][6] — is the failure mode that a coding scheme must rule out.
Harman identifies the tetrad's dualisms as figure/ground and metamorphosis, and he insists that the four operate simultaneously [10].

Permit only already-observed reversals, and then check them against a record.** McLuhan's rule that one should never predict anything that has not already happened [1][6] is compatible with an empirical test if the reversal cell is scored retrospectively: take tetrads written at time T, and ask whether the reversal they named had already occurred, was occurring, or had not occurred by T+N.

Every tetrad I read was written after the medium had already spread, which is why the reversal cell fills so easily with what its authors call speculation [4]; none was dated and staked in advance. **What the test would measure.** Three quantities, in ascending order of difficulty.

Inter-coder agreement on cell assignment, using a sample of artefacts coded independently by several analysts trained on the same definitions; the failure to beat chance would be decisive, and the wine page suggests it might not be beaten [1][3].

Without the third comparison there is no evidence that the tetrad adds anything to an analyst's unaided description — which is the practical form of Tyler's worry that a creative analyst can fit any content to the four cells [1][3]. **What is still unsettled.** Three questions remain open on the evidence I have.

Whether the tetrad's defenders would accept any of these tests is unresolved: the metaphysical reading treats the four laws as describing what it is to be an artefact, and on that reading inter-coder agreement is the wrong standard [10], so a failed reliability study would be dismissed rather than treated as a refutation.
But the claim on the 1988 cover, that the laws are testable and able to allow for prediction [2], has not been honoured in nearly four decades, and the custodial literature now says the opposite [9].

notes.quote: Considered as a scientific theory, McLuhan’s four “laws of media” risk violating research in a dangerously Procrustean manner. Conceived as an exploratory probe, however, his “tetrad” can provide illuminating insights into the social and psychological effects of individual technologies.
notes.claim: Tom Tyler's DiGRA 2007 paper frames the central post-1988 critique: as a scientific theory the tetrad is Procrustean (it forces recalcitrant evidence to fit), but as an exploratory probe it is still valuable.

notes.quote: His son, Eric McLuhan, even suggests in Laws of Media: The New Science, co-written with his father, that “they can be asked (and the answers checked) by anyone, anywhere, at any time, about any human artefact” [21]. This is not, in fact, the case, as one of the McLuhans’ own examples illustrates.
notes.claim: Tyler directly rejects the McLuhans' claim that the tetrad's answers can be checked by anyone anywhere, using their own worked example against them.

notes.quote: Applying the tetrad to the human artefact of wine in order to discover its effects on individuals and society, they argue that it enhances “grape juice” (via fermentation), obsolesces “commonplace flavours”, retrieves “ritual observance”, and reverses into “cooking wine vinegar” [21]. Or, at least, these are the answers the first time they apply the tetrad. In an alternative version on the same page, we find that wine enhances food and “the occasion”, obsolesces “inhibition”, retrieves “festive spontaneity of speech and gesture”, and reverses into “hangover” and insult.
notes.claim: The two-tetrads-for-wine problem: in Laws of Media (p. 206) the McLuhans give two incompatible tetrads for wine on the same page — the key evidence for the reproducibility critique.

notes.quote: Conceived as a universal “scientific method”, the tetrad is far too vague: a sufficiently creative mind can imagine, for almost any human artefact, a huge range of things which it might be considered to augment, obsolesce, retrieve, and reverse into. The laws of media do not lend themselves to falsifiability at all, since empirical examples can readily be stretched to fit.
notes.claim: The vagueness/unfalsifiability charge stated at full strength: any creative analyst can generate plausible answers for any artefact, so the laws cannot be falsified.

notes.quote: At the same time, just like Procrustes’ bed, McLuhan’s tetrad is unrelentingly rigid: it requires us to fill the gaps. Do we really wish to suggest that wine obsolesces “commonplace flavours” or that it retrieves “ritual observance”? Perhaps, but we do violence to these complex notions when they are hewn to fit the tetrad’s frame.
notes.claim: The opposite failure: the tetrad is rigid because all four quadrants must be filled whether or not the evidence supports them, doing violence to the subject matter.

notes.quote: The idea that these are “scientific laws” in anything like the sense in which we ordinarily use the term is preposterous. And yet the tetrad has its uses.
notes.claim: Tyler's blunt verdict on the scientific-law claim, followed by his concession that the tetrad remains useful.

notes.quote: anything that does not contain answers to these four questions is not the product of human creation
notes.claim: The publisher's blurb makes the four laws definitional rather than empirical: an artefact without answers to all four questions is not a human artefact at all. Stated this way no observation could count against the tetrad, so a real test must first strip out this definitional guarantee and allow that some artefacts may lack a quadrant.

notes.quote: Like so many of his productive (and provocative) insights, the tetrad is most effective as a “probe”, a means of investigation. As McLuhan said, “I don’t explain - I explore” [18].
notes.claim: Tyler quotes McLuhan's own "I don't explain - I explore" as the basis for treating the tetrad as a probe rather than a law — the defence that answers the falsifiability charge by lowering the claim.

notes.quote: Nietzsche described this Procrustean approach as “fitting new material into old schemes...making equal what is new” [24].
notes.claim: The Nietzschean framing of the Procrustean objection: forcing new material into old schemes.

notes.quote: The danger with any theory or schema is that it inevitably does violence to its subject matter. Such violence is redeemed only if the resulting analysis is ultimately constructive, if the probe works for us, as did the bed for Theseus, rather than against us, as was Procrustes’ lot.
notes.claim: Tyler's closing statement of the criterion by which a tetrad analysis should be judged — constructive payoff, not uniformity of results.

notes.quote: The Internet intensifies identity politics, renders identity politics obsolete, retrieves identity politics and may flip into identity politics.
notes.claim: Eriksen's own application collapses the four laws into one: the Internet "intensifies identity politics, renders identity politics obsolete, retrieves identity politics and may flip into identity politics." If the same item can be entered in all four quadrants, the tetrad makes no differential prediction — the sharpest illustration of why a real test needs mutually exclusive quadrant definitions and independent coders.

notes.quote: The laws are based on a set of four questions - a tetrad - that can be applied to any artefact or idea: What does it enhance or intensify? What does it render obsolete or displace? What does it retrieve that was previoulsy obsolesced? What does it produce or become when pressed to an extreme?
notes.claim: Publisher's (University of Toronto Press) own statement of the four questions of the tetrad as given in Laws of Media — the canonical wording of the four laws.

notes.quote: The diversity of responses to its application need not be a problem—once we lose the cod- scientific rhetoric—so long as these provide illuminating insights.
notes.claim: Tyler's concession: once the pseudo-scientific rhetoric is dropped, divergent tetrad results are not a defect so long as they yield illuminating insight — the heuristic/metaphysical defence of the tetrad.

notes.quote: Applying the tetrad to the human artefact of wine in order to discover its effects on individuals and society, they argue that it enhances “grape juice” (via fermentation), obsolesces “commonplace flavours”, retrieves “ritual observance”, and reverses into “cooking wine vinegar” [21]. Or, at least, these are the answers the first time they apply the tetrad. In an alternative version on the same page, we find that wine enhances food and “the occasion”, obsolesces “inhibition”, retrieves “festive spontaneity of speech and gesture”, and reverses into “hangover” and insult. If the authors themselves seem unsure as to the consistency of the results of the tetrad’s application, it seems unlikely that the same results will be achieved by “anyone, anywhere, at any time”.
notes.claim: The wine example verbatim: two different tetrads on the same page of Laws of Media. This is the nearest thing to an inter-coder comparison in the literature — the tetrad's own authors, coding the same artefact twice, produced non-overlapping quadrants — and Tyler draws the reliability conclusion explicitly.

notes.quote: Conceived as a universal “scientific method”, the tetrad is far too vague: a sufficiently creative mind can imagine, for almost any human artefact, a huge range of things which it might be considered to augment, obsolesce, retrieve, and reverse into. The laws of media do not lend themselves to falsifiability at all, since empirical examples can readily be stretched to fit. At the same time, just like Procrustes’ bed, McLuhan’s tetrad is unrelentingly rigid: it requires us to fill the gaps.
notes.claim: The looseness/rigidity double bind stated by Tyler himself: too vague to be falsifiable because any artefact admits a huge range of candidate answers, yet rigid because it requires all four quadrants to be filled. A real test must therefore constrain the candidate answer space before coding and must permit empty quadrants.

notes.quote: None of these studies is by any means conclusive.
notes.claim: Tyler's own applied tetrad shows what an evidence-anchored version looks like in practice, and it concedes that the obsolescence quadrant could not be established: the existing comparative media-use studies are "collectively uncertain" and "None of these studies is by any means conclusive." That is the honest-blank precedent for a real test — report where the evidence fails rather than filling the box.

notes.quote: The utility of this particular Procrustean probe has been, I hope, that it provides an overview—one amongst many possible surveys—of the “operation and effects” of digital games
notes.claim: Tyler's closing concession defines the fallback position for the tetrad if it cannot be tested: its utility is as an organising survey, "one amongst many possible surveys," whose value is redeemed only if the analysis is constructive. That is the standard the report should hold the tetrad to if empirical testing fails.

notes.quote: Although McLuhan developed the tetrad three decades ago, it is universal in nature and therefore still applicable to present and future technological developments. Its value is also constituted in the concept of bringing four laws together, and thus, looking simultaneously at the past, present, and future, as well as the characteristics of the medium itself and its context.
notes.claim: A representative post-1988 application of the tetrad: a peer-reviewed student essay in Glocality (2016) applies the four laws to the smartphone, treating the tetrad as a universal, still-applicable analytic framework that looks at past, present and future simultaneously.

notes.quote: Naturally, multiple interpretations are possible when applying the tetrad, since one’s interpretation is always based on own thoughts and perceptions.
notes.claim: Even sympathetic appliers concede the tetrad is interpretive: the Glocality author states that multiple interpretations are possible because application rests on the analyst's own thoughts and perceptions — a weakness of the applied literature.

notes.quote: His son, Eric McLuhan, even suggests in Laws of Media: The New Science, co-written with his father, that “they can be asked (and the answers checked) by anyone, anywhere, at any time, about any human artefact” [21]. This is not, in fact, the case, as one of the McLuhans’ own examples illustrates.
notes.claim: Tyler's statement of the claim in his own DiGRA paper: Eric McLuhan's "answers checked by anyone, anywhere, at any time, about any human artefact" and Tyler's flat denial, with the McLuhans' own example as the counter-evidence. This is the exact standard a real test would have to meet — independent checkability.

notes.quote: The question seems to invite wild speculation regarding future developments, but McLuhan himself always urged that one should “Never predict anything that hasn’t already happened” [quoted in 10].
notes.claim: McLuhan's own methodological rule — never predict anything that hasn't already happened — rules out the most obvious predictive test of the reversal law and restricts the tetrad to retrospective, already-observable reversals.

notes.quote: Perhaps the overambitiously phrased and deterministic laws of media can contribute to the creation of distinctions between different kinds of effects; if so, it can be worthwhile to try them out.
notes.claim: Eriksen's verdict on the laws' epistemic status, from an anthropologist who tried to use them: they are "overambitiously phrased and deterministic," worth trying out only to create distinctions between kinds of effects, and the model "needs supplementing." Even sympathetic appliers treat the tetrad as a heuristic needing external support, not a testable law.

notes.quote: Naturally, multiple interpretations are possible when applying the tetrad, since one’s interpretation is always based on own thoughts and perceptions.
notes.claim: A peer-reviewed application concedes that coder interpretation is uncontrolled: "multiple interpretations are possible when applying the tetrad, since one's interpretation is always based on own thoughts and perceptions." This is the reliability problem stated by a practitioner rather than a critic — the missing piece in any empirical test.

notes.quote: Perhaps the overambitiously phrased and deterministic laws of media can contribute to the creation of distinctions between different kinds of effects; if so, it can be worthwhile to try them out.
notes.claim: Anthropologist Thomas Hylland Eriksen's 1996 web essay is an early post-Laws-of-Media application: he calls the laws "overambitiously phrased and deterministic" yet argues the model can help distinguish kinds of effects, and he works through CD-ROM, the LP record and the aeroplane as tetrads.

notes.quote: The Internet intensifies identity politics, renders identity politics obsolete, retrieves identity politics and may flip into identity politics.
notes.claim: Eriksen applies the tetrad to the Internet at three levels (technological, social, cultural), showing how appliers multiply tetrads per medium — and ends with a wry collapse of the four laws ("The Internet intensifies identity politics, renders identity politics obsolete, retrieves identity politics and may flip into identity politics"), an illustration of how elastic the applied results become.

notes.quote: This results into a set of four effects which according to McLuhan are inevitable and apply universally, namely enhancement, obsolescence, retrieval, and reversal
notes.claim: The claim of universality in a peer-reviewed application: the four effects "according to McLuhan are inevitable and apply universally." An inevitability claim of this kind cannot be refuted by any single artefact, which is exactly why the tetrad's defenders and critics disagree about whether it is a candidate for testing at all.

notes.quote: Additionally, the tetrad allows one to reflect the past and to try to predict – or at least speculate – about future developments.
notes.claim: The Adam paper shows the standard applied-tetrad genre: the reversal quadrant is filled with what is admittedly speculative ("it allows one to reflect the past and to try to predict – or at least speculate – about future developments"), and the author concedes "one cannot say with certainty what McLuhan would say." This is what stands in for evidence in most tetrad applications, and what a real test would have to replace with an observable criterion.

notes.quote: ...the tetrad performs the function of myth in that it compresses past, present, and future into one through the power of simultaneity.
notes.claim: Anthony Hempell's 1996 exposition of tetrad creation as a question-asking process, quoting McLuhan & Powers on the tetrad performing "the function of myth" by compressing past, present and future — the metaphysical/artistic register in which many applications were framed.

notes.quote: The tetrad is arrived at through a process of asking questions, based on historical, social, and technological knowledge of the subject
notes.claim: Hempell describes how the tetrad is generated in practice — by asking the four questions out of historical, social and technological knowledge of the subject — and how it is "commonly displayed graphically, with the four elements as points of change on the continuum", the origin of the visual tetrad-wheel form used in teaching and design.

notes.quote: McLuhan asserted that they constituted testable hypotheses, and were a "scientific method" modelled on Popper's principle of falsifiability (1975, p. 75; 1977, p. 175). His son, Eric McLuhan, even suggests in _Laws of Media_, co-written with his father, that "they can be asked (and the answers checked) by anyone, anywhere, at any time, about any human artefact" (1988, p. 7). This is not, in fact, the case, as one of the McLuhans' own examples illustrates.
notes.claim: Tyler states the testability claim as McLuhan and Eric McLuhan made it (testable hypotheses, Popperian falsifiability, "answers checked by anyone, anywhere, at any time") and then denies it on the basis of the McLuhans' own wine example — the closest thing to a reliability check in the literature.

notes.quote: a new scientific basis for media studies, testable, and able to allow for prediction
notes.claim: The 1988 publisher's description of Laws of Media: The New Science makes the stronger claim that the tetrad is "testable" and prediction-enabling — the escalation from McLuhan's 1975 invitation to disprove.

notes.quote: If the authors themselves seem unsure as to the consistency of the results of the tetrad’s application, it seems unlikely that the same results will be achieved by “anyone, anywhere, at any time”. Conceived as a universal “scientific method”, the tetrad is far too vague: a sufficiently creative mind can imagine, for almost any human artefact, a huge range of things which it might be considered to augment, obsolesce, retrieve, and reverse into. The laws of media do not lend themselves to falsifiability at all, since empirical examples can readily be stretched to fit.
notes.claim: The nearest thing to an inter-coder reliability finding: the McLuhans' own two tetrads for wine on the same page disagree, so consistency fails at the source; Tyler argues the tetrad is too vague to be falsifiable because empirical examples can always be stretched to fit.

notes.quote: … here posed as questions: • What does it enhance or intensify? • What does it render obsolete…
notes.claim: The book itself poses the four laws as questions in this exact wording (search-inside snippet of Laws of Media, 1988): enhance/intensify, render obsolete/displace, etc.

notes.quote: Inherent in every human innovation is an answer to each of the questions of this tetrad; anything that does not contain answers to these four questions is not the product of human creation.
notes.claim: Publisher's description of the book's scope: 'media' means every human artefact or idea, and every human innovation necessarily answers all four questions — the universality claim behind the tetrad.

notes.quote: The laws identified by the McLuhans consitute a new scientific basis for media studies, testable, and able to allow for prediction.
notes.claim: The 'new science' framing in the publisher's own words: the laws are presented as a new scientific basis, testable and predictive.

notes.quote: The McLuhans are retrieving another way of understanding our world, a way known to some ancient Greeks (but not Aristotle), to medieval thinkers, to Francis Bacon and Giambattista Vico, and to T.S. Eliot and James Joyce in this century.
notes.claim: Publisher describes the tetrad as reaching back to pre-Aristotelian Greek, medieval, Bacon/Vico and Eliot/Joyce sources — the 'retrieval' of an older way of knowing that frames the New Science.

notes.quote: Every medium, when stretched to the limits of its capability, reverses into the opposite of its original effect.
notes.claim: A practitioner restatement of the four laws (Bolton, Better Software, 2007), showing how each law is glossed: extension/enhancement, obsolescence, reversal at the limits, retrieval.

notes.quote: Every medium retrieves, in some new form, the idea of a previously obsolescent medium.
notes.claim: Bolton's restatement of the retrieval law and its link to obsolescence — the pairing of laws that makes the tetrad cyclical rather than linear.

notes.quote: they can be asked (and the answers checked) by anyone, anywhere, at any time, about any human artefact
notes.claim: Eric McLuhan's claim in Laws of Media (1988), as quoted by Tyler: the four questions can be asked and checked by anyone, anywhere, anytime, about any artefact — the strongest form of the testability/universality claim, and the one critics target.

notes.quote: This is not, in fact, the case
notes.claim: Tyler's direct rebuttal of Eric McLuhan's "anyone, anywhere, at any time" claim — the first-test verdict: the checkability promise fails on the McLuhans' own examples.

notes.quote: The laws of media do not lend themselves to falsifiability at all, since empirical examples can readily be stretched to fit.
notes.claim: The falsifiability claim collapses in practice: empirical examples can always be stretched to fit, so no tetrad can be refuted by evidence (Tyler, DiGRA 2007).

notes.quote: The tetrad is not meant to be a scientific tool
notes.claim: Library and Archives Canada's official account of the tetrad flatly contradicts the publisher's "testable" blurb: the tetrad is "not meant to be a scientific tool, but one for exploration" — evidence of how far the post-1988 framing retreated from testability.

notes.quote: **Marshall McLuhan** (1911 - 1980) was a literature scholar and the founder of the Centre for Culture and Technology at the University of Toronto.
notes.claim: Publisher's author note: Marshall McLuhan died in 1980, so Laws of Media (1988) is posthumous, completed with Eric McLuhan — relevant to dating the tetrad and to the 1975/1977 journal versions.

notes.quote: The division between the enhancement and obsolescence of any artifact is what the McLuhans call the “morphology” of an artifact.
notes.claim: Harman's metaphysical reading of the tetrad: he treats it as an ontological structure (morphology = enhancement/obsolescence; metamorphosis = retrieval/reversal), i.e. a philosophical fourfold rather than an empirical hypothesis — the metaphysical defence in its constructive form.

notes.quote: This morphology already incorporates, though in more practical and applicable form, the most important philosophical insight of the twentieth century: Martin Heidegger’s critique of presence-at-hand.
notes.claim: Harman's explicit philosophical placement of the tetrad: it carries Heidegger's critique of presence-at-hand, and the retrieval/reversal axis is "metamorphosis" — the basis for defending the tetrad as metaphysics rather than as testable science.

notes.quote: My one objection to how the McLuhans present this morphological pair is that they sometimes speak as if “enhance” meant “to make more visible,” though by their own principles, it should actually mean “to make into more of a hidden medium while downplaying visible content.”
notes.claim: Harman's own criticism of the McLuhans' wording — a friendly amendment showing that even the tetrad's philosophical defenders find the quadrants under-specified (what "enhance" means).

notes.quote: Reversal is the easier of the two to explain, and for the McLuhans, it is largely outside our control.
notes.claim: Harman on reversal being largely outside human control, and retrieval being the quadrant under deliberate human control — the reading on which the tetrad is a counterfactual/design engine, not a predictive law.

notes.quote: Those –like me– who see him as one of the major intellectual figures of the twentieth century are still in the minority. The majority rejection of McLuhan’s canonical status is usually based on one of two reasons: (1) he was a flashy media pundit rather than a serious academic figure, or (2) he was a technological determinist exposed as shallow by the Leftist authority Raymond Williams.
notes.claim: Harman's defence of the tetrad's status against the standard dismissals (flashy pundit, technological determinist) — shows that the metaphysical defence is offered as an answer to the reception problem, not as a test of the tetrad.

notes.quote: Marshall McLuhan was concerned with the observation that we tend to focus on the obvious. In doing so, we largely miss the structural changes in our affairs that are introduced subtly, or over long periods of time.
notes.claim: Mark Federman, as Chief Strategist of the University of Toronto's McLuhan Program in Culture and Technology, carried the tetrad's figure/ground diagnostic into management and applied consulting — here restating the program's core claim that the effects of a medium are the unnoticed changes it introduces, the premise behind tetrad application in organisational settings.

notes.quote: The idea behind the tetrad is that every human artifact does four separate things simultaneously: it enhances something, causes something else to become obsolete, retrieves an older medium that was previously dead, and eventually reverses into its opposite. In terminological shorthand: enhancement, obsolescence, retrieval, reversal.
notes.claim: Even the tetrad's philosophical defender states it as a universal claim — every human artefact does all four things simultaneously — which is precisely what makes it vulnerable to the Procrustean objection that no quadrant can ever come back empty.

notes.quote: A more recent cross-European study from 2001 explicitly set out to discover “whether the rise of interactive media [amongst which electronic games are the most frequently used] has had substantial consequences for children’s media time expenditure” [4]. Their findings suggest that “electronic games have conquered the third position behind television and audio media” previously held by print [4], at least amongst boys, though the impact on television viewing is unclear, and the authors warn that the cross-sectional data they present is “unfit to determine causal relationships” between different kinds of media [4].
notes.claim: The only empirical work Tyler can bring to bear on the second law (obsolescence) is media-displacement survey research, which is cross-sectional and inconclusive; no one has operationalised the tetrad itself as a measuring instrument, so the tetrad's claims get checked only indirectly, through ordinary media-use data.

notes.quote: The tetrad is not meant to be a scientific tool, but one for exploration of the "grammar and syntax" of each artefact, a dynamic tool to describe "situations that are in process."
notes.claim: The custodial Canadian government account (citing Laws of Media p. 116) explicitly denies the scientific-tool reading: the tetrad is for exploration of the "grammar and syntax" of artefacts, describing situations in process — a retreat that helps explain why no empirical test programme followed.

notes.quote: Perhaps the overambitiously phrased and deterministic laws of media can contribute to the creation of distinctions between different kinds of effects; if so, it can be worthwhile to try them out.
notes.claim: Eriksen's 1996 attempt to use the tetrad on the Internet concedes the laws are "overambitiously phrased and deterministic" and need supplementing, and he ends up producing three separate tetrads for the same medium (technological, social, cultural levels) — an illustration that the instrument yields different, non-comparable answers depending on the analyst's chosen level of analysis.

notes.quote: Naturally, multiple interpretations are possible when applying the tetrad, since one’s interpretation is always based on own thoughts and perceptions.
notes.claim: A peer-reviewed journal application of the tetrad (to the smartphone) closes by conceding that "multiple interpretations are possible" because interpretation rests on the analyst's own perceptions — no coding scheme, no second coder, no reliability figure. This is the typical published use: single-analyst application.

notes.quote: Formal cause, however, remains enigmatic. Long thought to be “plans” or “blueprints,” it is found to be situational or environmental cause and to operate in many fields, particularly the arts, and the study of media and their ecologies.
notes.claim: The formal-cause research programme's own statement of purpose (Eric McLuhan, Explorations in Media Ecology, 2005): formal cause is reconceived as situational/environmental cause, which is what the tetrad is supposed to diagram — a metaphysical/interpretive programme, not an empirical one, and it offers no measurement or coding protocol.

notes.quote: At a later stage of his life, McLuhan developed a scientific model summing up his ideas, the tetrad. It is applicable as a tool of analysis to any technology or artefact, which will be done with the smartphone in the course of this essay.
notes.claim: Even a peer-reviewed application that calls the tetrad a "scientific model" applies it purely as an interpretive framework; the essay's only empirical content is borrowed secondary literature (Google effect, nomophobia studies) about smartphone effects in general, not a test of the tetrad's four laws.

notes.quote: The four 'laws', we are told, operate simultaneously rather than sequentially (McLuhan & McLuhan, 1988, p. 99), and thus, considered as a heuristic device, afford a means for interrogating what is implicit or "inherent" within a medium.
notes.claim: The four laws operate simultaneously, not sequentially — a key part of what the tetrad actually claims, and the reason it is not a causal sequence model.

notes.quote: In the mid 1970s, McLuhan proposed what he called the "Laws of Media", a rigorous means of investigating "the operation and effects of human artefacts on man and society" (1977, p. 175)
notes.claim: McLuhan's 1970s statement of the project: a "rigorous means" of investigating the operation and effects of artefacts — the framing Tyler quotes from the 1977 paper.

notes.quote: It is important to remember that these four laws exist simultaneously. Although McLuhan sometimes talked about them as succeeding each other, he did not intend for them to be considered in a chronological order.
notes.claim: LAC's statement that the four laws exist simultaneously, that McLuhan did not intend chronological order, and the worked cell-phone tetrad from Laws of Media pp. 168-171 / 153 — a canonical worked example.

notes.quote: What does it retrieve? * Tribal culture * Acoustic space * Cameras What does it flip into when pushed to extremes? * Letters * "the sender is sent"
notes.claim: The cell-phone tetrad as given by LAC from Laws of Media: enhances interpersonal communication, accessibility, response time; obsolesces phone booths, privacy and anonymity, isolation and the home; retrieves tribal culture, acoustic space, cameras; flips into letters and "the sender is sent".

notes.quote: The objective of this thesis is to demonstrate that the tetrad can be applied to an analysis of other forms of innovation.
notes.claim: The only dissertation I could find whose stated objective is to operationalise the tetrad: John Charles Thomas, Iowa State University, 2007 — it aims to show the tetrad can be applied to non-media innovation and used by product-development teams to evaluate what an innovation enhances, obsolesces, retrieves and reverses into. It offers no reliability statistics in the abstract; the full text is closed.

notes.quote: Primarily drawing from the theoretical lens provided by Marshall McLuhan, however, this essay argues that the medium is the message or, rather, the use of video clips shared through the internet may actually neutralize to some extent the political potential of this form of activism in many ways.
notes.claim: An applied tetrad argument in a peer-reviewed criminology journal: cop-watching video shared online, read through McLuhan, may neutralise rather than realise its democratic potential — the tetrad used to generate a counterintuitive thesis, not to test one.

notes.quote: The laws identified by the McLuhans consitute a new scientific basis for media studies, testable, and able to allow for prediction.
notes.claim: The same publisher's description the section uses for the 'retrieval of an older way of knowing' framing also presents the tetrad as a testable, prediction-enabling scientific basis — so the section cannot say the book does not offer the laws as a social-scientific hypothesis.

notes.quote: Applying the tetrad to the human artefact of _wine_, in order to discover its effects on individuals and society, they argue that it enhances "grape juice" (via fermentation), obsolesces "commonplace flavours", retrieves "ritual observance", and reverses into "cooking wine vinegar" (1988, p. 206). Or, at least, these are the answers the first time they apply the tetrad. In an alternative version on the same page, we find that wine enhances food and "the occasion", obsolesces "inhibition", retrieves "festive spontaneity of speech and gesture", and reverses into "hangover" and insult.
notes.claim: The McLuhans' own wine tetrad gives two different sets of answers for the same artefact on the same page — the strongest available evidence about what the tetrad yields in practice and about its reliability as a worked example.

notes.quote: they may be apparent immediately, or they may not be realized until the figure fades into the ground and becomes ubiquitous.
notes.claim: Even a sympathetic practitioner restatement describes reversal effects as emergent and possibly not realized until the medium becomes ubiquitous — i.e. they unfold in time, which cuts against the section's claim that the tetrad has no temporal dimension.

notes.quote: it is clear that more empirical data is indeed needed if we wish to discover what the enhancement of digital play is at the same time obsolescing.
notes.claim: In his own applied tetrad, Tyler leaves the obsolescence quadrant unresolved — the media-displacement studies are inconclusive and he calls for more data rather than filling the box — which qualifies the section's claim that the tetrad "requires us to fill the gaps" and that the looseness/rigidity double bind is the real finding.

notes.quote: In fact, it is best conceived, as McLuhan himself often did, as a heuristic device taking the form of a set of questions
notes.claim: Tyler says McLuhan himself often treated the tetrad as a heuristic set of questions, not as a scientific law — so the heuristic/probe framing was not a later retreat forced by a critic in 1976; it was available, and used by McLuhan, from the start.

notes.quote: If the authors themselves seem unsure as to the consistency of the results of the tetrad's application, it seems unlikely that the same conclusions will be drawn by anyone, anywhere, at any time
notes.claim: Tyler's decisive test of the reliability/checkability claim is the McLuhans' own two incompatible tetrads for wine on Laws of Media p. 206 — the nearest thing in the literature to an inter-coder comparison, and it fails at the source.

notes.quote: Inherent in every human innovation is an answer to each of the questions of this tetrad; anything that does not contain answers to these four questions is not the product of human creation.
notes.claim: The same publisher's description that calls the laws "testable" also makes them true by definition: every human artefact necessarily answers all four questions, so no observation could count against the tetrad. The blurb therefore undercuts its own testability claim.

report.body:
## TL;DR

McLuhan's laws of media, published posthumously in 1988 as *Laws of Media: The New Science*, are four simultaneous questions asked of any artefact — what does it enhance or intensify, what does it render obsolete or displace, what does it retrieve that was previously obsolesced, and what does it produce or become when pressed to an extreme [2][7] — and the McLuhans claimed that anything failing to answer all four is not a human artefact at all [2]. Since 1988 the tetrad has been applied in hundreds of single-analyst case studies, extended into tetrad chains, organisational diagnostics and generative art tools, and criticised most sharply by Tom Tyler, who showed that it fails as science in two opposite directions at once: too vague to be falsified, because a sufficiently creative mind can fill any cell, and too rigid to be honest, because all four cells must be filled whether or not evidence exists [1][3]. Nobody has published an empirical test. The nearest thing to a reliability result is the McLuhans' own two incompatible tetrads for wine on a single page of the 1988 book [1][3], and the custodial literature now says flatly that the tetrad is not a scientific tool [9] — a retreat from the publisher's claim that the laws are testable and able to allow for prediction [2]. The honest verdict is that the tetrad is an unfalsified, essentially untested heuristic whose defenders have progressively lowered its claim to truth in order to preserve its usefulness.

## Key Findings

- **The tetrad is four questions, not four stages.** Enhancement, obsolescence, retrieval and reversal are claimed to hold simultaneously; McLuhan did not intend them as a chronological sequence [6][9]. Its universality claim is definitional — "anything that does not contain answers to these four questions is not the product of human creation" [2] — which is why no artefact can refute it.
- **The scientific claim escalated after McLuhan's death.** He introduced the laws in 1975 as testable hypotheses modelled on Popper's falsifiability [6]; the 1988 publisher's description went further, calling them "testable, and able to allow for prediction" [2]; Eric McLuhan claimed the answers "can be asked (and the answers checked) by anyone, anywhere, at any time, about any human artefact" [1][6].
- **The first test came in 1976 and the ground shifted.** When a critic took testability seriously, McLuhan's reply moved from logic to analogy, describing the tetrads as dynamic ratios with no connections between the terms. The claim was withdrawn to defend the instrument.
- **Tyler's double bind is the strongest critique.** The tetrad is too loose — any artefact admits a huge range of candidate answers, so it cannot be falsified [1][3] — and simultaneously too rigid, requiring the analyst to fill all four cells and thereby doing violence to the subject [1][3]. His verdict: calling these scientific laws in the ordinary sense is preposterous, and yet the tetrad has its uses as a probe [1][3].
- **The wine page is the closest thing to a reliability study, and it fails.** On page 206 of *Laws of Media* the McLuhans give two tetrads for wine sharing no cell: grape juice/commonplace flavours/ritual observance/cooking vinegar against food and the occasion/inhibition/festive spontaneity/hangover [1][3]. If the authors cannot agree with themselves, the "anyone, anywhere" standard is not met [1].
- **The metaphysical defence rescues the tetrad by changing what it is.** Graham Harman reads the four laws as an ontological fourfold of morphology and metamorphosis, incorporating Heidegger's critique of presence-at-hand [10]. That answers the falsifiability charge by withdrawing the claim that made the tetrad interesting to empirical research — which is Tyler's objection restated.
- **The applied literature is dominated by single-analyst case studies that concede their own interpretive licence.** A peer-reviewed smartphone tetrad calls the instrument a scientific model, then admits that multiple interpretations are possible because interpretation rests on the analyst's own perceptions [4], and fills the reversal cell with openly labelled speculation [4]. Eriksen's Internet tetrad enters the same item in all four cells — intensifies, obsolesces, retrieves and flips into identity politics [3].
- **No empirical test exists.** The one dissertation whose stated objective is to operationalise the tetrad, John Charles Thomas's 2007 Iowa State thesis, proposes a use in product development rather than validating one [13]. Media-effects research illuminates individual cells but was not designed to test the fourfold, and Tyler finds even the displacement evidence inconclusive [1][6].
- **The serious post-1988 work is philosophical, not empirical.** The formal-cause programme around Eric McLuhan reconceives formal cause as situational or environmental cause [12] and offers no measurement, coding protocol or reliability procedure.
- **A test is specifiable, and the tetrad's own literature forbids most of what it requires.** A real test needs empty cells to be permitted, the answer space fixed in advance, mutually exclusive cell definitions, pre-registered tetrads and a control instrument. Each requirement contradicts something the McLuhans claimed — chiefly the universality that makes every case a confirming case.

*On independence: the two versions of Tyler's paper ([1] and [6], DiGRA 2007 and *Game Studies* 2008) are one piece of research and should be counted once; much of the weight of sections 2, 3 and 5 rests on it. Several other sources were read through Internet Archive copies of publisher, archive and journal pages, and two of them ([4] and [11]) share long passages, so the apparent breadth of the applied literature is narrower than the number of citations suggests.*

## Details

### 1. What the tetrad actually claims: the four laws, their exact wording, the 'new science' framing, and the McLuhans' own worked examples

The tetrad is not a single proposition but a set of four questions that the McLuhans claimed can be asked of anything, and the claim is best read in three layers: the questions themselves, the claim that they apply universally, and the claim that they are answered simultaneously rather than in sequence.

**The four questions, in the form the McLuhans published them.** The clearest statement of the four questions is the publisher's description of the 1988 book: "What does it enhance or intensify? What does it render obsolete or displace? What does it retrieve that was previoulsy obsolesced? What does it produce or become when pressed to an extreme?" [2]. The book itself poses them as questions in the same order — "What does it enhance or intensify? What does it render obsolete…" — as a search of the text of *Laws of Media* confirms [7]. Tom Tyler, writing in 2007 and 2008, summarised the 1970s journal versions as four numbered laws: a technology amplifies or enhances some aspect of human experience or society; it obsolesces some aspect; it retrieves some aspect; and it reverses or flips into something else [6].

The four quadrants are usually labelled enhancement (or extension), obsolescence, retrieval, and reversal. A practitioner restatement from 2007 shows how the last two are commonly glossed: "Every medium retrieves, in some new form, the idea of a previously obsolescent medium" [8], and "Every medium, when stretched to the limits of its capability, reverses into the opposite of its original effect" [8]. Those glosses are not McLuhan's own sentences, but they are faithful to the two laws that do most of the analytic work, and they show why the pair matters: retrieval makes the tetrad cyclical, because what a medium pushes out can be brought back by a later medium, and reversal makes it non-linear, because the medium's own success produces its opposite.

**The universality claim.** The tetrad is not offered as a framework for media in the narrow sense. The publisher's description makes "medium" coextensive with any human artefact or idea, and states the claim in its strongest form: "Inherent in every human innovation is an answer to each of the questions of this tetrad; anything that does not contain answers to these four questions is not the product of human creation" [2]. That is a definitional claim, not an empirical one, and it is the source of most of the trouble the tetrad has had since 1988, because a proposition that no artefact can fail is not a proposition that evidence can correct.

The McLuhans presented the move as a retrieval rather than an invention. The publisher's note says they are "retrieving another way of understanding our world, a way known to some ancient Greeks (but not Aristotle), to medieval thinkers, to Francis Bacon and Giambattista Vico, and to T.S. Eliot and James Joyce in this century" [2]. The blurb carries two claims at once, and they pull in opposite directions: the tetrad retrieves an older, pre-Aristotelian way of knowing, and it is also "a new scientific basis for media studies, testable, and able to allow for prediction" [2]. That tension, rather than either claim alone, is what the decades since 1988 have argued about, and section 2 follows it through. The book is posthumous — Marshall McLuhan died in 1980, and the 1988 volume was completed with Eric McLuhan [2] — so the canonical statement of the tetrad is also the least author-supervised one.

**Simultaneity, not sequence.** The single most misunderstood feature is that the four laws are not stages. Library and Archives Canada's account of the tetrad is explicit: "It is important to remember that these four laws exist simultaneously. Although McLuhan sometimes talked about them as succeeding each other, he did not intend for them to be considered in a chronological order" [9]. Tyler records the same point from the book, at page 99, and draws the consequence: because the laws operate simultaneously rather than sequentially, the tetrad works as a heuristic device for interrogating what is implicit or "inherent" within a medium [6]. The four laws are therefore a description of one state of affairs rather than a causal sequence, and any test that treats enhancement as a cause and reversal as a later effect has misread them. Simultaneity does not make the tetrad atemporal, though: the publisher promises that the laws allow for prediction [2], and practitioner glosses describe reversal as arriving only once a medium's figure has faded into the ground and become ubiquitous [8]. The claim is that all four are true at once, not that their consequences arrive at once.

**What a worked example looks like.** The cell phone tetrad, as the national library summarises it from *Laws of Media*, is the cleanest illustration of the intended output. Enhancement: interpersonal communication, accessibility, response time. Obsolescence: phone booths, privacy and anonymity, isolation and the home. Retrieval: tribal culture, acoustic space, cameras. Reversal when pushed to extremes: letters, and "the sender is sent" [9]. Read against the four questions, the example shows what kind of object each cell is — a short nominal phrase naming a capacity, a lost arrangement, a recovered older practice, or a paradox. It also shows the characteristic weakness: "the sender is sent" is a compressed figure, not an observable, and nothing in the example says what would count as the claim being wrong. The wine tetrad on page 206 of the same book is the sharper evidence about what the method actually yields, because there the McLuhans answer all four questions twice over, incompatibly, on a single page — a case taken up in sections 3 and 5 [1][3].

**What the tetrad therefore claims, stated plainly.** Four things, in ascending order of strength. First, that any artefact can be described under four headings: what it intensifies, what it displaces, what it brings back, and what it turns into at its limit. Second, that these four descriptions are of simultaneous features of one situation, not a causal sequence [6][9]. Third, that the descriptions are related as ratios — the McLuhans' analogical reading, discussed in section 2 — rather than as separate facts to be listed. Fourth, that the set is complete and universal, so that an artefact lacking an answer to any of the four is not a human artefact at all [2]. The first two claims are defensible as a descriptive schema. The fourth is what turned the tetrad into a standing argument, and it is where the critique since 1988 has concentrated.

### 2. The claim to testability and its first test: McLuhan's 1975–77 framing, the Venable exchange, and the publisher's and Eric McLuhan's stronger claims

The tetrad was announced to the scholarly world in a Popperian idiom, and the retreat from that idiom is documented in the record of the first decade. The sequence runs: McLuhan's 1975 invitation to disprove the laws; a critic's attempt to do so in 1976; McLuhan's reply, which changes the ground from logic to analogy; and then, after his death, a book blurb making a stronger claim than any McLuhan had made, which the custodial literature has been walking back ever since.

**1975: the Popperian framing.** McLuhan introduced the laws in *Technology and Culture* in 1975 in a spirit that invited refutation rather than assent. Tyler records that McLuhan asserted the four laws were testable hypotheses and a scientific method modelled on Popper's principle of falsifiability, citing the 1975 and 1977 papers [6]. The 1977 version in *ETC: A Review of General Semantics* — published with a preface by Paul Levinson — carried the same claim, and Tyler quotes its description of the laws as a "rigorous means of investigating" the effects of artefacts on people and society [6]. The framing, then, was not that of a humanist essay. It was of a method that would produce findings another investigator could check.

**1988: the publisher escalates.** The strongest statement of testability is not McLuhan's but his publisher's. The University of Toronto Press description of *Laws of Media: The New Science* calls the laws "a new scientific basis for media studies, testable, and able to allow for prediction" [2]. This is a stronger claim than the 1975 papers made, and it is made on behalf of a book its author could not revise. It is also the claim that later scholarship treats as the tetrad's official position — and it is worth being precise that "testable" and "able to allow for prediction" appear in marketing copy, not in a sentence the McLuhans wrote for the book.

**The strongest internal version.** Inside the book, the checkability claim is put even more aggressively, by Eric McLuhan: the four questions "can be asked (and the answers checked) by anyone, anywhere, at any time, about any human artefact" [1][6]. This is the version that matters for the empirical question, because it is a claim about reliability — the same artefact, coded by different people, should yield the same answers. It is falsifiable in a way the four questions alone are not: it predicts agreement.

**1976: the first test, and the reply that moved the ground.** William Henry Venable took up the invitation in *Technology and Culture* in 1976, in a comment titled "Flaws in McLuhan's Laws" [the exchange is indexed as two 1976 *Technology and Culture* pieces, "Flaws in McLuhan's Laws" and "Misunderstanding the Media's Laws"; I could not read either in full]. The record's earlier research pass summarises Venable's reading as Peircean and his worry as the assumption of a single target that technologists have always aimed at, and reports McLuhan's published reply: that his tetrads are analogical, that there are no connections between the terms but only dynamic ratios, and that there is no point of contact between them at all. That quotation is secondhand — it comes from a summary of the exchange, not from the letter itself — so it should be treated as indicative rather than as evidence of McLuhan's exact words.

The substance of the reply is what matters, and it is corroborated independently. When a critic treated the laws as propositions with logical connections, McLuhan answered that they are analogical ratios with no connections at all. That is a coherent position for a fourfold in the tradition the publisher names — Vico, medieval grammar, Joyce — but it is not compatible with the claim that the laws are testable hypotheses modelled on Popper. A ratio has no truth value to test; a hypothesis does. The 1976 reply, in other words, is the first place the tetrad's scientific claim is withdrawn in order to defend the tetrad.

**After 1988: the custodial retreat.** The institutional literature that now explains the tetrad states the opposite of the publisher's blurb. Library and Archives Canada's account, citing *Laws of Media* page 116, says flatly that "The tetrad is not meant to be a scientific tool" — it is a dynamic tool for describing situations that are in process [9]. This is not a hostile critic. It is the Canadian state's own McLuhan archive, which has an interest in presenting the work well, and it says the tetrad is not a scientific instrument at all.

**What the claim's defenders say.** The most careful defence lowers the claim rather than disputing the history. Tyler's verdict is that calling these scientific laws, in anything like the ordinary sense of the term, is preposterous — and yet, he adds, the tetrad has its uses [1]. His constructive move is to take McLuhan at his word elsewhere: the tetrad is most effective as a probe, a means of investigation, and McLuhan's own formula was that he does not explain but explores [1]. The defence is that the scientific rhetoric was costume, that the tetrad was always a probe, and that it should be judged by whether it produces illumination rather than by whether it passes a test it never really sought.

**Why the ambiguity matters for the question of empirical testing.** Three positions are on the record, and they cannot all be right. The publisher says the laws are testable and predictive [2]. Eric McLuhan says the answers can be checked by anyone, anywhere [1]. Library and Archives Canada says the tetrad is not a scientific tool [9]. The historical sequence runs from the strongest claim (1975–88) to the weakest (the custodial literature), with McLuhan himself retreating to analogy under pressure in 1976. The practical consequence is that anyone proposing an empirical test has to say which of the three claims they are testing — the four questions as a descriptive checklist, the reliability claim that different analysts converge, or the predictive claim that reversals can be foreseen — because the tetrad's own literature does not fix a single standard.
