Section 5 takes the reliability claim as the one worth testing, since it is the only one stated precisely enough to fail.

### 3. The critique since 1988: vagueness, Procrustean rigidity, the two-tetrads-for-wine problem, and the metaphysical defence

The critique since 1988 has a small number of load-bearing arguments, and almost all of them were in place by the early 1990s. The most-cited is Tom Tyler's, and its distinctive contribution is that it identifies two opposite failures in the same instrument rather than one.

**The two-tetrads-for-wine problem.** Tyler's paper, first given at DiGRA in 2007 and later republished in *Game Studies*, attacks the checkability claim with the McLuhans' own example. In *Laws of Media*, at page 206, they apply the tetrad to wine twice on the same page. In the first version, wine enhances grape juice (through fermentation), obsolesces commonplace flavours, retrieves ritual observance, and reverses into cooking wine vinegar. In the second, wine enhances food and the occasion, obsolesces inhibition, retrieves the festive spontaneity of speech and gesture, and reverses into hangover and insult [1][3]. The two tetrads share no quadrant. Tyler draws the inference directly: if the authors themselves seem unsure about the consistency of the results, it seems unlikely that the same results will be achieved by anyone, anywhere, at any time [1]. This is the closest thing in the literature to an inter-coder reliability finding, and it is a failure at the source: the instrument's own designers, coding the same artefact, produced non-overlapping answers within a single page.

**Failure one: too loose.** Tyler's first objection is that the tetrad cannot be falsified because the space of admissible answers is unbounded. His sentence is worth having in full because it is the version later critics quote: as a universal scientific method, the tetrad is far too vague, since "a sufficiently creative mind can imagine, for almost any human artefact, a huge range of things which it might be considered to augment, obsolesce, retrieve, and reverse into" [1][3]. Nothing an artefact does can rule out a tetrad, because some analyst can always find a candidate for each cell. The looseness is not incidental: it follows from the analogical reading McLuhan adopted in 1976, in which the four terms are ratios rather than propositions.

**Failure two: too rigid.** The opposite failure is less often noticed and more damaging for practice. Because the tetrad claims that every artefact answers all four questions, the analyst must fill all four cells whether or not there is anything to put in them. Tyler's formulation: "it requires us to fill the gaps" [1][3]. He then tests this against the wine example, asking whether we really want to say that wine obsolesces commonplace flavours or retrieves ritual observance, and answering that the analysis does violence to these complex notions when they are forced into the tetrad's frame [1][3]. He names the move with Nietzsche's phrase about fitting new material into old schemes — making equal what is new [1][3]. The double bind is the real finding: an instrument that is simultaneously unfalsifiable (any answer is admissible) and coercive (an answer must be produced) cannot be corrected by evidence in either direction.

**The verdict, and the concession.** Tyler's summary judgement is that calling these scientific laws in anything like the ordinary sense is preposterous — followed immediately by the concession that the tetrad has its uses [1][3]. What it is good for, on his account, is redirecting attention to an artefact's operation and effects rather than to its content, and organising a field's existing findings well enough to show where researchers have been looking in the wrong place. His closing standard is aesthetic and pragmatic rather than epistemic: "The danger with any theory or schema is that it inevitably does violence to its subject matter" [1], and that violence is redeemed only if the resulting analysis is constructive — if the probe works for us as the bed did for Theseus rather than as it did for Procrustes [1][3]. Once the scientific rhetoric is dropped, he argues, divergent tetrads for the same artefact are not a defect so long as they yield illuminating insight [1][3]. That is a coherent position, but note what it concedes: the tetrad's value is now independent of its truth, and two incompatible tetrads for the same medium are both acceptable.

**The metaphysical defence.** The strongest counter-argument to Tyler does not dispute his reading of the wine page; it denies that the tetrad was ever a candidate for empirical testing. Graham Harman's essay on the McLuhans and artifact retrieval treats the four laws as an ontological structure rather than a hypothesis. On his reading, enhancement and obsolescence together constitute what the McLuhans call the morphology of an artefact, while retrieval and reversal constitute its metamorphosis [10]. The morphology, he argues, already incorporates in practical form Heidegger's critique of presence-at-hand — the point that a thing's readiness-to-hand is not exhausted by its measurable properties [10]. If that is what the tetrad is, then asking for inter-coder agreement is a category mistake: the tetrad is a philosophical fourfold describing what it is for something to be an artefact at all, not an instrument for generating predictions about particular artefacts.

Harman's defence has three features worth recording, because they set the terms for any later attempt to make the tetrad empirical. First, he states the universality claim as strongly as the publisher does: "every human artifact does four separate things simultaneously" — it enhances something, makes something else obsolete, retrieves a previously dead medium, and eventually reverses into its opposite [10]. Second, he supplies the test that any fourfold must pass, which is that its four cells be generated by crossing two prior dualisms; a fourfold whose underlying distinctions are shallow is decoration, however elegant. His own identification of the tetrad's dualisms is morphology — the pairing of enhancement with obsolescence — and metamorphosis, the pairing of retrieval with reversal [10]. Third, he offers a friendly correction to the McLuhans' own wording: they sometimes write as though "enhance" meant making something more visible, whereas on their own principles it should mean making something into more of a hidden medium while downplaying its visible content [10]. That is a philosopher's amendment, but it has an empirical consequence: if enhancement typically works by concealment, then the analyst's report of what a medium enhances is systematically the least reliable cell, not the most.

Harman also draws a distinction that matters for the testing question. Reversal, he says, is largely outside our control, while retrieval is the cell in which deliberate human agency operates [10]. That reads the tetrad as a counterfactual design instrument — a way of asking which possible worlds a medium has quietly killed — rather than as a predictive law. It also explains why the reversal cell is where tetrad applications most often drift into speculation, a point taken up in section 5.

**Why Harman's defence does not settle the dispute.** The metaphysical reading rescues the tetrad from Tyler's falsifiability charge by withdrawing the claim that made it interesting to a social scientist. If the four laws describe the structure of artefactuality, they cannot be wrong about wine, or about the cell phone, or about anything — which is precisely Tyler's first objection restated in philosophical vocabulary. The disagreement between Tyler and Harman is therefore not about evidence but about what kind of object the tetrad is. Harman is explicit that the stakes include McLuhan's academic standing: he notes that the majority rejection of McLuhan's canonical status rests on either the charge of flashy punditry or the charge of technological determinism exposed by Raymond Williams [10], and his essay is partly an argument that both charges misread the work. That is a defence of McLuhan's importance, not a demonstration that the tetrad works.

**The other criticisms, briefly.** Two further lines recur. The determinism charge — that the tetrad's language of what a medium does leaves no room for users — is the one Harman attributes to Williams and answers by pointing to the retrieval cell's dependence on human choice [10]. The vagueness charge is sometimes put as a charge of rhetoric rather than of method: the four cells are named with abstract nouns whose reference shifts between examples, so that "obsolescence" covers both the disappearance of phone booths and the suppression of privacy, which are different kinds of event. Neither line has generated a decisive rebuttal, and neither has been operationalised: no published critique that I found attempts to show empirically that the four cells cannot be distinguished by independent analysts. The critique remains, in that sense, philosophical.

### 4. How scholars applied and extended it: Levinson's tetrad wheels, Logan, Federman, Strate, Harman, and the design and game-studies uses

The applied literature is large, repetitive and mostly weak. The most sustained book-length extension is Robert K. Logan's *Understanding New Media: Extending Marshall McLuhan* (2010; second edition 2016), which takes figure/ground and the tetrad as the organising frame for a survey of digital media; I located the book and its reviews but did not read the text, so I record it as the central work of the extension literature rather than reporting its arguments. Of the programmes I could read, three separate out: the chaining of tetrads through time, the use of the tetrad as a diagnostic in organisations and design, and the single-analyst case study that has become the genre's default. Only the second has produced anything resembling a method.

**Chaining: from a fourfold to a sequence.** The most-cited formal extension is Paul Levinson's proposal of "tetrad wheels", in which one tetrad's reversal becomes the next medium's point of departure so that a series of fourfolds describes a historical trajectory. I could not verify this against Levinson's own text: it is reported in the record's earlier research pass, which cites a Lindia–Levinson article and a 1978 tetrad conference, and neither of those is in this report's notes. It is recorded here as a reported extension, not as a finding. Its interest is structural: it reintroduces sequence into an instrument whose four laws are supposed to operate simultaneously [6][9], which makes the tetrad usable for history at the cost of a construction the tetrad itself does not license.

**Anthropology: Eriksen's three-level tetrads.** The earliest substantial post-publication application I found is Thomas Hylland Eriksen's 1996 web essay, and it is unusually honest about the instrument's status. Eriksen calls the laws "overambitiously phrased and deterministic" and argues only that they may help create distinctions between different kinds of effects — if so, it can be worthwhile to try them out [3][6]. He then applies them to the Internet at three separate levels: technological, social and cultural. The move is significant because it multiplies the instrument: one medium now needs three tetrads, and there is no rule in the tetrad for deciding how many levels to distinguish. His essay ends with a deliberate reductio: "The Internet intensifies identity politics, renders identity politics obsolete, retrieves identity politics and may flip into identity politics" [3]. Eriksen's point is not that the tetrad is worthless but that its cells are elastic enough to receive the same content four times over. When that happens the tetrad makes no differential claim at all, and the analysis cannot be wrong about anything.

**Pedagogy and the visual form.** Anthony Hempell's 1996 exposition shows how the tetrad was taught, and why the applied literature looks the way it does. He describes the tetrad as arrived at by asking the four questions out of historical, social and technological knowledge of the subject [5], and notes that it is commonly displayed graphically with the four elements as points of change on a continuum [5]. He also quotes McLuhan and Powers on the tetrad performing the function of myth by compressing past, present and future into one through simultaneity [5]. That register — myth, simultaneity, compression — is the one in which most applications were written, and it explains the genre's characteristic form: a short essay, four bullet points, an arresting image in the reversal cell. The graphical wheel is a teaching aid, not a coding instrument; nothing in it tells a second analyst where to place an item.

**Organisational diagnosis: Federman and the McLuhan Program.** The most institutionally consequential application ran through the University of Toronto's McLuhan Program in Culture and Technology, where Mark Federman, as chief strategist, carried figure/ground and tetrad analysis into management consulting. Federman's restatement of the premise is the clearest statement of what the tetrad is for in that setting: McLuhan was concerned that "we tend to focus on the obvious", and in doing so we largely miss the structural changes introduced subtly, or over long periods of time [11]. Read this way the tetrad is a diagnostic for bringing an organisation's unnoticed environment into view. The figure/ground vocabulary here is Federman's, not Harman's: Harman's two generating dualisms are morphology and metamorphosis [10], and figure/ground is the perceptual pair the McLuhan tradition uses alongside them. This is the application with the strongest claim to practical value, and it is also the least falsifiable: a consultant's tetrad succeeds if the client finds it illuminating, and no record of disagreements between analysts is kept.

**Single-analyst case studies: the default genre.** The most common published use remains the four-cell case study, and a peer-reviewed example shows both its strengths and its limits. A 2016 essay in *Glocality* applies the tetrad to the smartphone, and its framing statements are representative of the whole genre. It calls the tetrad a "scientific model" and a tool applicable to any technology or artefact [4]; it asserts that McLuhan developed it late in life as a summing-up of his ideas [4]; it holds that although the tetrad was developed three decades earlier it is universal in nature and therefore still applicable to present and future technological developments, its value consisting in bringing the four laws together and so looking simultaneously at past, present and future, at the medium itself and at its context [4]. It also states the universality claim in its strongest form: the four effects are, according to McLuhan, inevitable and apply universally [4].

The essay's own admissions are what make it useful evidence about the method. It concedes that multiple interpretations are possible when applying the tetrad, since one's interpretation is always based on one's own thoughts and perceptions [4][6]. It fills the reversal cell with what it openly calls speculation — the tetrad allows one to reflect on the past and to try to predict, or at least speculate, about future developments [4] — and it concedes that one cannot say with certainty what McLuhan would say [4]. Its empirical content is entirely borrowed: studies of the Google effect and of nomophobia about smartphone effects in general, not evidence bearing on whether the four laws hold of the smartphone [4]. So the genre's structure is: a universal claim, four cells filled from the analyst's reading, borrowed evidence about the medium's effects in general, and an explicit disclaimer in the reversal cell.

**Games: Tyler's disciplined version.** The best applied tetrad I read is Tyler's own, and it is instructive precisely because it violates the genre's conventions. Each quadrant is anchored in cited research rather than in the analyst's impressions: enhancement engages Putnam's *Bowling Alone* and Arthur Asa Berger, and obsolescence engages cross-European media-use survey data and Nick Yee's MMORPG research. Where the evidence does not settle a cell he says so, concluding that the existing studies of whether games displace television are collectively uncertain and that none is by any means conclusive [1][6], and he then redefines obsolescence as remediation in the Bolter-and-Grusin sense rather than forcing the original claim. He narrows his scope deliberately at the outset, and though he later extends the enhancement analysis to multiplayer play, he claims modestly that the result is one amongst many possible surveys [1][6]. This is what an evidence-anchored tetrad looks like, and it required abandoning the universality claim in practice: the analyst must be allowed to leave a cell unresolved.

**Criminology and the counterintuitive thesis.** A 2014 *Surveillance & Society* article by Brian Schaefer and Kevin Steinmetz shows the tetrad used to generate a thesis against the grain of the field's assumptions. Drawing primarily on McLuhan, they argue that the medium is the message and that video clips of police actions shared through the internet may actually neutralise, to some extent, the political potential of cop-watching, so that caution is warranted about over-emphasising the power of video activism [14]. This is a good use of the instrument in Tyler's sense: the tetrad's job is to make an unexpected claim visible, and the article's contribution is the argument, not a demonstration that the four cells are correct.

**The most recent extension: generative and AI applications.** Two recent papers extend the tetrad into computational practice. A SIGGRAPH Asia 2023 art paper revisits the McLuhans' laws alongside the work of Ant Farm, and a 2026 *Leonardo* paper presents "Media Farm", a framework for AI-based reinterpretation and generation of conceptual media art inspired by McLuhan's tetrad and by Ant Farm's practices. I saw only the titles and abstracts of these through search listings and could not read either in full, so I record them as evidence of a live extension into generative systems rather than as findings. The direction is coherent with the tetrad's design: if the four cells are prompts, a language model can fill them fluently and at scale, which is exactly the "sufficiently creative mind" whose existence Tyler's looseness objection depends on [1][3]. A machine that always finds four plausible answers is the limiting case of the Procrustean problem, not a solution to it.

**What the applied literature collectively shows.** Across four decades the tetrad has been applied, in the sources I read, to wine, the cell phone, the Internet at three levels, CD-ROMs, LP records, aeroplanes, smartphones, digital games and cop-watching video. Search listings show further applications to video conferencing, Microsoft Teams, soundscape composition and laser cleaning machines, whose texts I did not read. Almost every application is by a single analyst, cites no second coder, and treats divergent results as a feature [4]. None that I found reports a disagreement between analysts resolved by evidence. The extensions that have lasted — Levinson's chaining, Federman's organisational diagnostic, Tyler's evidence-anchored survey — all change the instrument's status rather than confirming it: they treat the tetrad as a way of organising an inquiry, and they locate its value in the illumination produced rather than in the correctness of the four cells.

### 5. Has anyone tested it empirically? Coding instruments, inter-coder reliability, quasi-experiments, and the formal-cause research programme

The short answer is no: there is no published empirical test of the tetrad. What exists is a large applied literature that uses the tetrad interpretively, one dissertation whose stated aim was to operationalise it, a body of ordinary media-effects research that bears on single cells without ever testing the fourfold, and a philosophical research programme that explicitly declines to be empirical. I searched for reliability studies, coding schemes, expert panels, Delphi applications and quasi-experiments, and found none that treats the tetrad itself as the object of measurement.

**What would count as a test, and why the claim makes it possible.** The tetrad's own literature supplies a testable proposition even where its authors disclaim science: Eric McLuhan's claim that the four questions can be asked and the answers checked by anyone, anywhere, at any time, about any human artefact [1][6]. That is a reliability claim. It predicts that independent analysts, given the same artefact and the same four questions, will produce answers that converge — not identical wording, but at minimum agreement on what belongs in each cell and on whether a cell can be filled at all. A reliability study is the cheapest possible test of the tetrad, requiring only multiple coders and a sample of artefacts, and no one has published one.

**The nearest thing to a result: the authors disagree with themselves.** The wine page of *Laws of Media* is the closest the literature comes to an inter-coder comparison, and it is a failure. Two tetrads for the same artefact, on the same page, sharing no cell: enhancement is grape juice in one version and food and the occasion in the other; obsolescence is commonplace flavours against inhibition; retrieval is ritual observance against festive spontaneity of speech and gesture; reversal is cooking wine vinegar against hangover and insult [1][3]. Tyler's inference is the reliability conclusion stated in words: if the authors themselves seem unsure about the consistency of the results, it seems unlikely that the same results will be achieved by anyone, anywhere, at any time [1]. This is not a controlled study, and it is a single case, but it is the designers of the instrument failing their own checkability standard on their own example, and no defender of the tetrad has produced a competing reading of that page.

**Why no test programme followed.** Four features of the instrument explain the absence, and each is documented.

First, the universality claim makes the tetrad immune to disconfirmation by construction. If anything that lacks answers to the four questions is not a human artefact at all [2], then no artefact can supply a negative case. A proposition that no observation could refute is not a candidate for testing, and the tetrad's defenders state it in exactly this form: every human artefact does four things simultaneously [10], and the four effects are inevitable and apply universally [4].

Second, the cells are not mutually exclusive in practice. Eriksen's Internet example enters the same item in all four quadrants — the Internet intensifies identity politics, renders identity politics obsolete, retrieves identity politics and may flip into identity politics [3][6]. If one item can occupy every cell, the tetrad makes no differential prediction, and there is nothing for a coder to get right or wrong. Any real test would have to fix exclusion rules that the tetrad's own literature does not supply.

Third, the analysts' own reports concede that the answers are interpretive. The peer-reviewed smartphone application states that multiple interpretations are possible because one's interpretation is always based on one's own thoughts and perceptions [4][6] — a candid statement that the instrument's output is a function of the analyst. In the same essay the reversal cell is filled with what the author calls speculation about future developments [4], which is the cell where an empirical criterion would be most valuable and where it is most conspicuously absent.

Fourth, the methodological rule McLuhan imposed on himself forecloses the most obvious predictive test. He urged that one should never predict anything that has not already happened [1][6]. The reversal law is the tetrad's predictive cell — what the medium becomes when pushed to its extreme — and McLuhan's own rule restricts it to reversals already observable, which converts the test into retrospective redescription. That is a coherent position, but it means the tetrad cannot be scored against future events.

**The one sustained attempt at operationalisation.** The only work I found whose explicit objective is to make the tetrad operational is John Charles Thomas's 2007 Iowa State University dissertation, *Operationalizing McLuhan's tetrad to focus on innovation effects*. Its abstract states the aim plainly: the tetrad, historically limited to media theory, consists of four basic interrelated questions that McLuhan held to be fundamental to technologies, and "The objective of this thesis is to demonstrate that the tetrad can be applied to an analysis of other forms of innovation" [13]. The intended application is commercial: a product-development team, asking what an innovation enhances and then working through the remaining three cells, would be enabled to focus on the innovation's probable future effects and resultant consumer needs, giving planners and innovators a tool to reveal the consequences of innovation [13]. The abstract describes a design argument, not a validation: there is no mention of independent coders, of agreement statistics, or of a comparison between tetrad predictions and outcomes. The full text is closed access and I could not read it, so I cannot rule out that reliability data appear inside; on the evidence available, the dissertation proposes a use rather than testing one.

**Ordinary media research bears on single cells, never on the fourfold.** The obsolescence cell is the one most amenable to existing data, and Tyler's treatment shows how far such evidence gets. He reviews comparative media-use research, including a 2001 cross-European study that asked whether interactive media had substantially changed children's media time expenditure, and which found that electronic games had taken the third position behind television and audio media previously held by print, at least among boys, with the impact on television unclear; the authors warn that their cross-sectional data are unfit to determine causal relationships between media [1][6]. Tyler's conclusion is that none of these studies is by any means conclusive [1][6]. This is the pattern across the field: the tetrad's cells can be illuminated by media-effects research, but such research was designed to answer questions about displacement, attention or wellbeing, not to test whether an artefact answers all four questions simultaneously. Using it as evidence for the tetrad is post hoc.

**The formal-cause programme: a research programme that is explicitly not empirical.** The most substantial body of work built on the tetrad since 1988 is the formal-cause literature around Eric McLuhan and *Explorations in Media Ecology*. Its central statement, Eric McLuhan's 2005 article on formal cause, argues that formal cause, long thought to be plans or blueprints, is in fact situational or environmental cause operating in many fields, particularly the arts and the study of media and their ecologies. That is a metaphysical thesis about what kind of cause a medium is, and it is the theoretical ground the tetrad is supposed to diagram. It offers no measurement, no coding protocol and no inter-coder procedure. The programme is substantial — it has produced a journal literature on formal cause, quiddity and McLuhan's Aristotelianism, including a 2022 book by Laura Trujillo Liñán on formal cause in McLuhan's thinking — but it is a programme in philosophy of media, not in empirical media research, and it is where most of the serious post-1988 work on the tetrad actually lives.

**Adjacent empirical work that comes close.** Two studies use the tetrad in a group setting rather than as an object of test, and they are the nearest thing to empirical method in the applied literature. A 2024 *New Explorations* article by a soundscape-composition group marshals McLuhan's tetrad in a focus-group approach to music-based research, examining how soundscape composition may inform a specific community from an acoustic perspective; a 2023 *Explorations in Media Ecology* article applies the four laws to Microsoft Teams in the context of pandemic-era remote schooling. I read only the abstracts of these and cannot report their methods or whether either collects agreement data. Neither is described as a test of the tetrad. That is the state of play: where the tetrad meets empirical material, it is the analyst's lens, not the hypothesis under examination.

**The one empirical result that bears on the tetrad's use as a generative instrument.** There is a relevant finding from outside media theory, and it is about what happens when an instrument of this kind is run at scale by a fluent generator. Si, Hashimoto and Yang's ideation–execution study had 43 experts each spend over 100 hours executing randomly assigned research ideas; ideas generated by a language model, judged more novel than experts' ideas at pitch time, lost significantly more on every evaluation metric once executed, dropping roughly 1 to 2 points on a 10-point scale for novelty, excitement and effectiveness, while human ideas held steady. The record's earlier research pass reports this as evidence that a generator will always produce a fluent four-cell answer and that fluency at generation time does not predict value at evaluation time. I did not read that study directly for this report, so I cite it as reported there rather than as a primary finding, but it bears precisely on the tetrad's failure mode: a sufficiently creative mind can fill the cells, and filling them well is not the same as being right [1][3].

### 6. What a real test would require, and what is still unsettled about the tetrad

Because the tetrad has never been tested, the most useful contribution a report can make is to specify what a test would have to look like, and to say which parts of that specification the tetrad's own literature forbids. Four requirements follow directly from the failures documented above, and each of them requires abandoning something the McLuhans claimed.

**1. Strip out the definitional guarantee.** The publisher's statement that anything lacking answers to the four questions is not a product of human creation [2] has to go, because it makes every case a confirming case. A testable version must allow that some artefacts have empty cells, and must treat an empty cell as a possible result rather than a failure of analysis. Tyler's own tetrad is the model here: he reports that the evidence on whether games displace television is collectively uncertain and that none of the studies is by any means conclusive [1][6], and then redefines the cell rather than filling it. Any empirical programme that cannot record "no answer found" will reproduce the Procrustean problem exactly.

**2. Constrain the answer space before coding.** Tyler's looseness objection is that a sufficiently creative mind can imagine a huge range of candidates for any cell [1][3]. A test must therefore fix, in advance, the vocabulary in which answers may be given — the level of analysis (individual, household, institution, economy), the time horizon, and the kind of entity admissible in each cell. This is the step Eriksen's essay shows to be indispensable and missing: his three tetrads for the Internet at technological, social and cultural levels are not comparable, because no rule fixes the level [3][6]. Fixing the level is not a technicality; it is what makes two analysts' answers comparable at all.

**3. Make the cells mutually exclusive.** Eriksen's reductio — the Internet intensifies, obsolesces, retrieves and flips into identity politics [3][6] — is the failure mode that a coding scheme must rule out. The natural discipline is Harman's: if the four cells are generated by crossing two dualisms, then the two axes must be defined before any artefact is coded, and an item must be assignable to one axis or the other rather than to both. Harman identifies the tetrad's dualisms as figure/ground and metamorphosis, and he insists that the four operate simultaneously [10]. A test built on that reading would ask coders to classify each claimed effect as a figure/ground shift or a metamorphosis, and would count an item that fits neither as a coding failure.

**4. Permit only already-observed reversals, and then check them against a record.** McLuhan's rule that one should never predict anything that has not already happened [1][6] is compatible with an empirical test if the reversal cell is scored retrospectively: take tetrads written at time T, and ask whether the reversal they named had already occurred, was occurring, or had not occurred by T+N. This converts the tetrad's weakest cell into a checkable one without violating its own methodological prohibition. It also requires what the applied literature never provides — a dated, pre-registered tetrad. Every tetrad I read was written after the medium had already spread, which is why the reversal cell fills so easily with what its authors call speculation [4]; none was dated and staked in advance.

**What the test would measure.** Three quantities, in ascending order of difficulty. Inter-coder agreement on cell assignment, using a sample of artefacts coded independently by several analysts trained on the same definitions; the failure to beat chance would be decisive, and the wine page suggests it might not be beaten [1][3]. Predictive yield, using pre-registered reversal claims scored against a dated record. And differential value, comparing the tetrad's output with a control instrument — a plain effects checklist, or a figure/ground analysis without the fourfold — on the same artefacts, judged blind. Without the third comparison there is no evidence that the tetrad adds anything to an analyst's unaided description — which is the practical form of Tyler's worry that a creative analyst can fit any content to the four cells [1][3].

**What is still unsettled.** Three questions remain open on the evidence I have. Whether the tetrad's defenders would accept any of these tests is unresolved: the metaphysical reading treats the four laws as describing what it is to be an artefact, and on that reading inter-coder agreement is the wrong standard [10], so a failed reliability study would be dismissed rather than treated as a refutation. Whether the formal-cause programme could supply the operational definitions that the empirical literature lacks is unknown to me — I read its central statement but not the surrounding corpus, and its concern is with what kind of cause a medium is, not with how to code one. And whether the recent generative extensions change the picture is genuinely open: a system that produces four fluent cells on demand is the limiting case of Tyler's looseness problem, and the ideation–execution evidence reported in the record suggests that fluency at generation does not survive evaluation, but neither of the two computational papers I located was read in full, so I cannot say whether either reports validation.

**Where this leaves the tetrad.** The evidence supports a narrower conclusion than either camp claims. The tetrad has never been tested; the one reliability check available in its own pages fails; the research programme built on it since 1988 is philosophical rather than empirical; and its most careful users treat it as a probe whose value is independent of the truth of its four cells. That does not make it worthless — an instrument that reliably produces illuminating questions about artefacts is a real intellectual asset, and the applied literature shows it doing that across domains from wine to cop-watching video. But the claim on the 1988 cover, that the laws are testable and able to allow for prediction [2], has not been honoured in nearly four decades, and the custodial literature now says the opposite [9]. The honest description is that the tetrad is an unfalsified and largely untested heuristic whose defenders have, since 1976, progressively lowered its claim to truth in order to preserve its usefulness.


## Open questions

- **Nobody has run the cheapest possible test.** A reliability study needs only a sample of artefacts, several analysts and a coding scheme; it has not been published. The wine page is a single anecdotal failure, not a measured agreement statistic. Until someone reports inter-coder agreement, the question of whether the tetrad is reliable is unmeasured rather than settled.
- **Whether the tetrad adds anything over an unaided description is untested.** No study compares a tetrad analysis with a control instrument — a plain effects checklist, or figure/ground analysis without the fourfold — on the same artefacts, judged blind. Without that comparison, "illuminating" is a reader's report, not a finding.
- **The defensive position is not stated precisely enough to refute.** The metaphysical reading holds that the four laws describe what it is to be an artefact, so inter-coder disagreement would be a category mistake rather than a refutation [10]. No defender has said what observation, if any, would count against the tetrad, which leaves the dispute about its status unresolvable by evidence.
- **The formal-cause literature may already contain operational definitions and I did not read it.** I read Eric McLuhan's central 2005 statement [12] and located the surrounding journal corpus and a 2022 book on formal cause, but not the corpus itself. If operational criteria exist anywhere in the McLuhan tradition, that is where they would be.
- **The generative extension is unexplored.** Two recent papers apply the tetrad to AI-based media-art reinterpretation and generation; I saw only titles and abstracts. Whether a language model filling four cells on demand is a use of the tetrad or a demonstration of Tyler's looseness objection is an open and, given how such tools are now built, a practically important question.
- **Coverage was thin in three places.** I could not read the 1976 Venable–McLuhan exchange in *Technology and Culture* (the reply is reported secondhand from the record's earlier pass), could not obtain the full text of Thomas's 2007 dissertation, and could not read Levinson's own writing on tetrad wheels or Logan's *Understanding New Media*. Those are the three places where a claim in this report rests on a secondary report rather than a read text.
- **One flagged point I am leaving as it stands.** The report's account of the 1988 blurb holds both of its claims — retrieval of an older way of knowing and a testable new science — in tension rather than choosing one; the publisher's own sentences support the tension and I have quoted both.

## Beyond this question

For anyone who uses the tetrad as a working instrument — in design, in organisational diagnosis, or in an automated system that fills the four cells — the evidence points to four disciplines, each of which answers a documented failure rather than a stylistic preference.

**Allow empty cells and report them.** The rigidity Tyler identifies is not a critic's invention: the tetrad's own universality claim requires all four answers [2][10]. An analyst who records "no evidence" in a cell is doing the only thing that makes the instrument corrigible, and Tyler's own tetrad is the precedent — he reports that the displacement evidence is inconclusive rather than filling the box [1][6].

**Pre-register the tetrad and date it.** Because reversal is the cell that attracts speculation [4], and because McLuhan's own rule forbids predicting what has not already happened [1][6], the only honest use of the reversal cell is retrospective: name what has already flipped, and record when. A tetrad written after the fact describes; a tetrad written before and scored later tests something.

**Fix the level of analysis before starting.** Eriksen needed three tetrads for one medium because nothing in the instrument fixes whether the unit is a technology, a social practice or a cultural pattern [3]. Two analysts working at different levels will produce non-comparable answers and call the difference insight.

**Generate rival tetrads rather than one.** The wine page is usually read as an embarrassment. It is more useful read as a method: if two incompatible tetrads for the same artefact are both illuminating, the disagreement between them is the finding, and publishing both is more honest than choosing the better-sounding one. Tyler's own concession supports this — divergent results are acceptable once the scientific rhetoric is dropped, so long as they illuminate [1][3].

The wider point is about what kind of thing the tetrad is good for. As a candidate scientific law it has failed for nearly four decades, on its own authors' evidence. As a disciplined prompt for asking what an artefact intensifies, displaces, recovers and becomes, it has a track record across domains from wine to cop-watching video [14]. The mistake, in either direction, is to confuse the two — to claim the authority of science for a probe, or to dismiss a probe because it is not science.
